questions.stem: Which radiation does a smoke detector use?

options.explanation: Alpha ionises the air inside the detector.
Beta would pass through smoke.
Gamma would pass through smoke.
Neutrons are not used in detectors.

questions.stem: What triggers the smoke alarm circuit?

options.explanation: No gamma is involved.

options.text: the sensor no longer detecting the alpha-driven current
options.explanation: Smoke blocks the alpha, cutting the current.

options.text: a rise in the alpha current
options.explanation: The current falls, not rises, when smoke enters.
Heating is not the mechanism.

questions.stem: Why is beta suited to measuring foil thickness?

options.text: because beta passes through everything untouched
options.explanation: That is closer to gamma’s behaviour.

options.text: because beta ionises the foil chemically
options.explanation: No chemistry is involved.

options.text: because foil only partially absorbs beta, so the count rate tracks thickness
options.explanation: Partial absorption gives a usable signal range.

options.text: because beta is stopped entirely by any foil
options.explanation: Complete absorption would give a useless on/off signal.

questions.stem: Foil on the gauge line gets thicker. What happens to the detector count rate?

options.text: it increases, because thicker foil emits beta
options.explanation: The foil does not emit.
The signal’s whole point is to change.
Partial absorption keeps a nonzero count.

options.text: it decreases, because more beta is absorbed
options.explanation: Absorption rises with thickness.

questions.stem: Why would gamma be a poor choice for the foil gauge?

options.text: because nearly all gamma would pass through regardless of thickness
options.explanation: Gamma’s deep penetration removes the signal’s sensitivity.
Gamma is detectable.

options.text: because gamma would be fully absorbed
options.explanation: That is alpha’s problem.
Gamma is weakly ionising but that is not the issue here.

questions.stem: Describe how a smoke detector uses alpha radiation.
questions.modelAnswer: The alpha source ionises the air so a small current flows; smoke blocks the alpha, the current stops, and the alarm sounds.

questions.stem: State one medical and one industrial use of radioactivity.
questions.modelAnswer: Medical: radiotherapy for cancer (or tracers for diagnosis). Industrial: monitoring the thickness of foil (or smoke detection).

questions.stem: Explain why beta, rather than alpha or gamma, monitors aluminium foil thickness.
questions.modelAnswer: Foil partially absorbs beta, so count-rate changes track thickness; alpha would be absorbed completely at any thickness, and gamma would pass through almost unchanged — neither gives a usable signal.

questions.stem: A gauge reading rises above its set-point while making foil. Should the rollers press harder or ease off? Explain.
questions.modelAnswer: A higher count rate means fewer beta particles were absorbed, so the foil is too thin — the rollers must press harder to thicken it back to the set-point.

questions.stem: Which radiation treats cancer from outside the body?

options.explanation: Neutron therapy is not the named syllabus treatment.
Gamma beams penetrate deeply enough to reach tumours.
Alpha cannot penetrate skin.
Beta lacks the required depth.

questions.stem: Why are the gamma beams rotated around the patient?

options.explanation: Tracers are a separate diagnostic tool.
Rotation does not immobilise tissue.

options.text: to spread the entry dose over healthy tissue while concentrating dose on the tumour
options.explanation: Rotation protects the paths, not the target.
Rotation redistributes dose; it does not amplify it.

options.text: a beam of gamma aimed at a tumour
options.explanation: That is radiotherapy.

options.text: a device that detects radiation dose
options.explanation: That is a dosemeter/badge.
That is storage shielding.

options.text: a radioactive isotope whose emissions are tracked through the body
options.explanation: Tracers trace movement of substances like blood.

questions.stem: Why is gamma preferred for sterilising sealed instruments?

options.text: because it penetrates the packaging and irradiates all sides
options.explanation: Sealed packs can be treated without opening.

options.text: because it is the weakest ioniser so it is safest
options.explanation: Sterilisation needs the killing dose, not weakness.

options.text: because alpha could also pass through the pack
options.explanation: Alpha cannot even pass paper.
Irradiation does not make objects radioactive.

questions.stem: Irradiated food carries the Radura symbol. The treatment’s purpose is to…

options.explanation: Flavour is not the aim.

options.text: kill micro-organisms so the food keeps longer
options.explanation: Irradiation reduces food-borne organisms.

options.text: make the food radioactive for tracing
options.explanation: Food is not made radioactive.
No heating is involved.

questions.stem: Name the radiation used in radiotherapy and state why it is chosen.
questions.modelAnswer: Gamma rays are used because they penetrate the body deeply enough to reach the tumour.

questions.stem: Explain the role of a tracer in diagnosing cancer.
questions.modelAnswer: A tracer is a radioactive isotope introduced into the body; a PET scan detects its emissions to reveal the tumour’s location.

questions.stem: Explain why gamma, not beta, sterilises medical equipment inside sealed packaging.
questions.modelAnswer: Gamma’s deep penetration lets it pass through the wrapping and reach every surface of the instruments; beta would be stopped by the packaging and could not sterilise the contents.

questions.stem: A hospital needs to sterilise single-use syringes that are pre-sealed in plastic. Justify the choice of source and note one safety outcome for patients.
questions.modelAnswer: A gamma source is chosen because it irradiates through the sealed plastic from all sides, killing micro-organisms without unsealing; patients receive sterile syringes with no microbial contamination.
